abstract:
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is an emerging cause of chronic hepatitis in immunocompromised individuals. It remains unclear whether laboratory mice are susceptible to all known HEV genotypes, and the determinants of the HEV host range remain poorly understood. Given the numerous genetic variants and experimental tools available in mice, which permit mechanistic studies, we aimed to develop an inbred mouse model of HEV infection.
AG129 and C57BL/6J mice were infected with HEV. Infection was assessed by detection of HEV RNA using reverse-transcription PCR and RNAscope, liver function tests, and histopathological examination. Single-cell RNA sequencing and transcriptomic analysis were used to delineate infection dynamics and investigate virus-host interactions.
We show that an emerging human-pathogenic, rat-derived HEV-C1 strain can breach the species barrier and efficiently infect AG129 mice. Using single-cell RNA sequencing and RNAscope, we demonstrate viral tropism for liver macrophages and hepatocytes, providing a single-cell atlas of intrahepatic HEV-C1 infection. We subsequently adapted this HEV-C1 isolate by serial passage in AG129 mice. After 13 passages, the resulting mouse-adapted strain gained the ability to infect immunocompetent C57BL/6J mice. Both immunocompromised and immunocompetent mouse models supported efficient HEV replication and enabled antiviral and vaccine testing. CD4+ T-cell depletion experiments suggest that impaired CD4+ T-cell responses may contribute to the establishment of persistent infection.
We developed two mouse models using AG129 and C57BL/6J mice that support efficient HEV-C1 replication. This work establishes the first immunocompetent mouse model of HEV infection. These mouse models provide a platform for studying HEV immunopathogenesis, evaluating antivirals and vaccines, and investigating mechanisms of cross-species transmission.
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) research is hampered by the lack of suitable small-animal models, and our study fills this gap by establishing two mouse models, particularly the immunocompetent C57BL/6J mouse model, which should support the use of versatile genetic and immunological tools for deep mechanistic studies in the future. This study also provides a single-cell atlas of HEV infection dynamics, revealing intrahepatic viral tropism. We identified CD4+ T-cell depletion as a pivotal driver of chronic infection. These mouse models offer a robust platform for studying HEV immunopathogenesis, evaluating antivirals and vaccines, and investigating mechanisms of cross-species transmission.
